caa6_deviation_metric.answer: Z-score (vertexwise); Extreme value deviation score (global measure); FDR-corrected thresholding at p < 0.05
caa6_deviation_metric.reason: The paper clearly describes the deviation metrics used, including subject-specific Z-scores at each vertex and a global extreme value deviation score.
caa6_deviation_metric.supporting_text: we derived a normative probability map (NPM) that quantifies the deviation from the normative model for CT at each vertex. This was done by using the normative model to predict vertexwise estimates of CT for each individual participant, then estimating a subject-specific Z score... We thresholded the NPMs, correcting for multiple comparisons by controlling false discovery rate (FDR) at p < .05 within each participant... we estimated a summary score for each participant capturing the individual's largest deviation from the typical pattern... we estimated a maximum deviation for each subject by taking a trimmed mean of 1% of the top absolute deviations for each subject across all vertices and fit an extreme value distribution to these deviations.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Spearman correlation coefficients were computed between global and regional extreme deviations and ADOS-2/ADI-R symptom severity scores, with FDR correction at p < 0.05. Global deviations from the normative model were negatively associated with ADOS-2 repetitive behaviors (r = -0.21, p < 0.05 after FDR correction). Regional deviations were associated with symptoms in several brain regions, particularly showing associations with repetitive behavior severity in prefrontal regions in female subjects (multiple regions survived FDR correction). In male subjects, similar patterns were seen but did not survive multiple comparison correction except for the superior frontal region in ADI-R. Social interaction and communication scores had nominally significant associations in female subjects but did not survive FDR correction.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: The study found few case-control differences but revealed highly individualized patterns of cortical thickness deviations that were widespread across the brain in individuals with ASD, with deviations correlating with severity of repetitive behaviors.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The classical case-control analysis showed only two small regions of increased cortical thickness in superior frontal and parietal cortices that survived FDR correction. In stark contrast, the normative modeling approach revealed striking, widespread patterns of cortical atypicality at the individual level. These deviations were highly individualized across participants, distinct across different developmental stages, and associated with symptoms, especially repetitive behaviors. The top 15 most deviating individuals all belonged to the ASD cohort (p < 0.0005, binomial test), with highly individualized patterns regarding both brain regions and sign of deviation (some positive, some negative). Negative deviations were most prominent in children, while positive deviations were most prominent in adolescents and adults. Regional deviations correlated with symptom severity, particularly with repetitive behaviors in prefrontal regions (ADI-R and ADOS-2), especially in female subjects. The deviations primarily involved areas previously associated with ASD: medial cortex including cingulate and dorsomedial prefrontal regions, lateral prefrontal and parietal cortices, temporal cortices, and hippocampal formation. Surface area showed similar patterns with slight differences. Results were robust to inclusion of IQ, site, and Euler number as covariates.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study demonstrates that normative modeling is well suited for understanding heterogeneity in psychiatric disorders by charting individualized deviations relative to the normative range, rather than focusing on group-level effects. The approach reveals that the case-control paradigm, which focuses on the 'average ASD participant,' disguises considerable interindividual variation crucial for precision medicine. The findings support the notion that a subset of ASD participants follow different developmental trajectories than TD subjects, and that the trajectory each ASD participant follows is highly individualized. The study suggests that capturing and capitalizing on variation at the individual level is at the heart of precision medicine approaches. The authors note that relatively few deviations were detected in ASD with ID, though the small sample size limits strong conclusions.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: First, trajectories of brain development were based on cross-sectional rather than longitudinal data. Second, while the sample size is reasonable, larger samples would yield more precise model estimates. Third, registration to a standard adult template could potentially cause bias, though few deviations in TD cohort make this unlikely. Fourth, the study design does not permit strong inferences about confounding variables (moderate associations found between deviations and image quality metrics, which were also associated with childhood ASD symptoms, comorbid ADHD symptoms, and IQ), and direction of causality cannot be determined. Fifth, no manual edits were performed on cortical surface reconstructions, which eliminates one source of bias but may reduce surface reconstruction quality in some cases. Sixth, relatively small sample size for ASD with ID group (n=20) limits conclusions about differences between ASD with and without ID.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: The study represents one of the early applications of normative modeling to ASD, demonstrating the value of individual-level analysis over group-level case-control approaches. Data comes from the EU-AIMS Longitudinal European Autism Project (LEAP), a large multi-site study with harmonized acquisition protocols (ADNI sequence). Seven study sites were included across the UK, Netherlands, Germany, and Italy. The study design included four age/ability subgroups: (A) adults 18-30 years (IQ≥70), (B) adolescents 12-17 years, (C) children 6-11 years, and (D) adolescents and adults with ID 12-30 years (IQ 50-70). ASD diagnosis was based on combined ADI-R and ADOS-2, though individuals not reaching conventional cutoffs were not excluded. Up to 70% of ASD individuals have comorbid psychiatric conditions, and 30-50% are on stable medications; therefore comorbidities were not excluded to capture the natural heterogeneity of ASD. The GPR model used a covariance function combining linear and non-linear terms with automatic relevance determination parameters. The normative model was trained exclusively on TD participants (n=206) and then applied to ASD participants (n=321) and also back to TD participants under cross-validation. Post-hoc analyses showed moderate correlations between deviations and Euler number (quality metric), with EN also correlating with age and ADI symptom domains. The study references prior work by Marquand et al. (2016) on normative modeling methodology and Wolfers et al. (2018) on application to schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Funding was provided by multiple EU grants including EU-AIMS, NWO VIDI grants, and Wellcome Trust.
